title: ENGR 206 Local Guided Practice
description: A complete offline test-file example. It is test content, not a parameterized problem generator.

teaching.whatToNotice: The output is measured across one resistor in a simple series chain.
teaching.whyThisOperation: The voltage divider formula gives the requested branch voltage once the source, selected resistor, and full series resistance are known.
commonMistakes: Using the upper resistor as R_load when the target is across the lower resistor.
Mixing kilo-ohms and ohms before forming the ratio.

teaching.whatToNotice: A single resistor has a known current and resistance.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Ohm's law turns the branch current and resistance into the branch voltage drop.
commonMistakes: Multiplying a value in kilo-ohms by amps without converting units.
Using total source voltage when the question asks for a resistor voltage.

teaching.whatToNotice: The voltage across and current through the same element are known.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Power is the product of the element voltage and current; the sign convention tells whether the element absorbs or supplies it.
commonMistakes: Using a current from a different branch.
Ignoring the marked current direction when interpreting the sign.

problems.title: Voltage divider with a unit conversion

prompt.text: Find the voltage at node a relative to ground. The output is measured across R2.

visual.altText: A 12 volt source feeds resistor R1 then node a. Resistor R2 connects node a to ground. The target is node a voltage relative to ground.

teaching.whyNow: The two resistor values must use the same unit before we add or ratio them.
teaching.whatToNotice: R1 is given in ohms, while R2 is given in kilo-ohms.
teaching.whyThisOperation: This conversion makes the resistance values directly compatible for the next arithmetic step.
teaching.inputMeaning: The selected value is R2, the lower resistor across which the target voltage is measured.
teaching.resultUse: The converted R2 value can be added to R1 to form the full series resistance.
commonMistakes: Treating 2 kilo-ohms as 2 ohms.
Converting R1 instead but forgetting to use that converted value later.

teaching.whyNow: The voltage divider needs the whole series resistance in its denominator.
teaching.whatToNotice: R1 and R2 are in one continuous path with no branch between them.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Series resistors add directly once their units match.
teaching.inputMeaning: R1 is the upper resistor and converted R2 is the lower resistor; both are part of the same current path.
teaching.resultUse: R_T is the denominator of the voltage-divider ratio.
commonMistakes: Using the parallel-resistance rule for a series circuit.
Adding values that are still in different units.

solutionPath.title: Apply the voltage divider to R2

teaching.whyNow: All three inputs for the divider are now available, so the requested node voltage can be calculated.
teaching.whatToNotice: Node a is the top of R2 and R2 is connected to ground, so V_a is the voltage across R2.
teaching.whyThisOperation: The divider returns the fraction of the source voltage across the selected lower resistor.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the 12 V source, R2 as the selected load resistor, and the combined R1 plus R2 total.
teaching.resultUse: This result is the requested target, so it can be stated as the final answer.
commonMistakes: Putting R1 in the numerator even though the target is across R2.
Using only R2 in the denominator.

teaching.whyNow: The target value has been calculated with its unit.
teaching.whatToNotice: The prompt asks for node a relative to the ground symbol.
teaching.whyThisOperation: A final answer should name the requested quantity, value, and unit.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the computed node voltage rather than one of the intermediate resistance values.
commonMistakes: Reporting 8 with no unit.
Reporting the source voltage instead of node a voltage.

prompt.text: A 24 ohm resistor carries 0.50 A. Find its voltage drop and the power it absorbs.

visual.altText: A current arrow of 0.50 amperes passes from left to right through a 24 ohm resistor with a positive voltage reference on the left side.

teaching.whyNow: Power needs voltage and current, and only current is directly given.
teaching.whatToNotice: The current and resistance refer to the same single resistor.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Ohm's law converts the known current and resistance into the missing voltage.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the branch current through this resistor and this resistor's own resistance value.
teaching.resultUse: The voltage can now be paired with the current in the power formula.
commonMistakes: Using a voltage from another component.
Forgetting that 0.50 times 24 is 12.

teaching.whyNow: Both quantities required by the power relationship are now known for the same element.
teaching.whatToNotice: The current enters the marked positive voltage side, so passive sign convention calls this absorbed power.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Multiplying element voltage by element current gives its power.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the 12 V result across this resistor and the original 0.50 A through it.
teaching.resultUse: This is the requested power target.
commonMistakes: Using the resistance instead of current in p = vi.
Mixing the current direction with the voltage reference.

teaching.whyNow: The requested power has been calculated and interpreted using the marked reference directions.
teaching.whatToNotice: The prompt asks for power, not just the voltage drop.
teaching.whyThisOperation: The final statement pairs the numerical result with the physical interpretation.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the calculated resistor power, not the source or an intermediate voltage.
commonMistakes: Leaving off watts.
Calling positive passive-sign-convention power supplied.

prompt.text: A point moves along the x direction with the following position function. Find its instantaneous velocity at t = 4 s.

visual.altText: A three-dimensional coordinate frame shows a point moving in the positive x direction. The x axis is highlighted and an arrow labels the velocity direction.

derivativeActions.title: Differentiate position with respect to time

teaching.whyNow: The requested quantity is instantaneous velocity, which is the slope of the position function at that time.
teaching.whatToNotice: The problem gives position x(t) but asks for velocity, not displacement.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Differentiating position with respect to time produces velocity before we substitute t = 4 seconds.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the stored position expression and select time t as the differentiation variable.
teaching.resultUse: The resulting velocity function can be evaluated at the stated time to reach the numerical answer.
commonMistakes: Substituting t = 4 into position before differentiating.
Calling 3t squared plus 2t a velocity function.

teaching.whyNow: We need the slope of the position curve before we can know the velocity at one instant.
teaching.whatToNotice: The target says instantaneous velocity and the supplied function is position.
teaching.whyThisOperation: Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time.
teaching.inputMeaning: Differentiate x(t) with respect to t, not with respect to x or another variable.
teaching.resultUse: The velocity function is ready to evaluate at t = 4 seconds.
commonMistakes: Using the original position value as the answer.
Dropping the factor of 2 when differentiating 3t squared.

solutionPath.title: State the instantaneous velocity at 4 seconds

teaching.whyNow: The derivative has been evaluated at the requested time.
teaching.whatToNotice: The requested output has velocity units, metres per second.
teaching.whyThisOperation: A final answer identifies the function value, number, and correct unit.
teaching.inputMeaning: Use the numerical evaluation of the velocity function at t = 4 seconds.
commonMistakes: Reporting 26 metres rather than metres per second.
Reporting the symbolic velocity function without evaluating it.
